title: What if you fell into Jupiter?
hook: What if you fell into Jupiter?
camera: locked vertical shot from slightly above and behind a lone astronaut in a white spacesuit with an orange backpack, falling face-down with arms and legs spread, small in the exact center of the frame, the surroundings filling the frame to every edge, the top third of the frame darker and calmer, left free for titles
objection: Wait, when do you hit the ground?
cta: How deep would you make it?

beats.caption: 1,321 Earths fit inside
beats.vo: What if you fell into Jupiter? It's so big that one thousand three hundred Earths would fit inside.
beats.state: deep black space full of stars, the striped orange, cream and brown disk of Jupiter filling the lower two thirds of the frame, the Great Red Spot visible below the astronaut, warm orange light on the suit
beats.fact_source: NASA Jupiter facts: about 1,321 Earths would fit inside Jupiter

beats.caption: 170,000 km/h fireball
beats.vo: You hit the air at a hundred seventy thousand kilometers per hour. It turns to plasma, hotter than the Sun's surface. Say your suit survives.
beats.state: the astronaut wrapped in a blinding orange-white plasma shell, long streaks of fire trailing up toward the top of the frame, the striped cloud tops close below, black sky above
beats.fact_source: NASA Galileo probe (1995): entry at 47.4 km/s (about 170,000 km/h), shock plasma about twice as hot as the Sun's surface

beats.caption: Ammonia ice, −110 °C
beats.vo: Zero kilometers, the cloud tops. White clouds of ammonia ice, at a hundred and ten degrees below zero.
beats.state: the fire gone, the astronaut falling through bright white and pale cream ammonia ice clouds, tiny ice crystals glittering around the suit, a thin layer of frost on the suit, pale blue haze above
beats.fact_source: NASA: Jupiter's top cloud layer is ammonia ice; about -110 °C at the 1 bar level

beats.caption: Water clouds and lightning
beats.vo: Eighty kilometers down, clouds of water. Lightning flashes all around you, and it's getting warmer.
beats.state: dark blue-grey storm clouds of water vapor all around, several bright branching lightning bolts lighting the clouds from inside, rain droplets streaking past the astronaut
beats.fact_source: NASA Juno: lightning in Jupiter's water clouds; water clouds lie roughly 50-100 km below the cloud tops

beats.caption: NASA's probe died here
beats.vo: A hundred fifty kilometers. This is where NASA's Galileo probe went silent: twenty three times Earth's pressure, a hundred fifty degrees.
beats.state: thick amber-brown haze, dim orange light from below, the astronaut's suit glowing faintly red with heat, steam rising off it, a small broken metal probe tumbling in the haze beside the astronaut
beats.fact_source: NASA: the Galileo probe transmitted for 58 minutes, down to about 150 km, 23 bar and 153 °C

beats.caption: Wait, where's the ground?
beats.vo: Wait, when do you hit the ground? Never. Jupiter has no surface. The gas just gets thicker, until it's a hot ocean.
beats.state: a dense dark-red glowing fluid all around, no clouds, slow swirling currents, the astronaut suspended and sinking slowly, a deep red glow from far below
beats.fact_source: NASA: Jupiter has no solid surface; gas grades into a hot, dense liquid

beats.caption: Hydrogen turns into metal
beats.vo: Twenty thousand kilometers. The pressure is over a million times Earth's. Hydrogen turns into a liquid metal.
beats.state: a shimmering silvery liquid metal ocean all around, mirror-like rippling surfaces reflecting orange light, electric blue sparks crackling through it, the astronaut's suit crumpled and cracked
beats.fact_source: NASA Juno: below about 1-2 million bar, hydrogen becomes liquid metallic hydrogen

beats.caption: Core: 24,000 °C
beats.vo: The core: twenty four thousand degrees, four times hotter than the Sun's surface. So, what if you fell into Jupiter?
beats.state: a blinding white-orange glowing core filling the bottom of the frame, intense heat waves, only a tiny dark silhouette of the astronaut left in the center, dissolving into the light
beats.fact_source: NASA: Jupiter's core temperature is about 24,000 °C (43,000 °F); the Sun's surface is about 5,500 °C
